result: Premature eye opening in ferrets causes profound alterations in temporal frequency tuning, characterized by increased low-pass responses and broadened temporal frequency bandwidths. EO1contra and EO2 cells exhibited significantly elevated low-pass index values (0.35 and 0.33 vs. 0.20 in controls) and all early-opened groups showed significantly wider absolute temporal frequency bandwidths (4.7-5.1 octaves vs. 4.1 octaves in controls, p<0.002).
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C32-C46, and C111-C115 provide converging quantitative evidence from electrophysiological recordings with appropriate statistical analyses (Linear Mixed Effects Models). The data show consistent patterns across multiple measures (low-pass indices, bandwidths, L50/H50 cutoffs) with significant p-values. The findings are supported by visual representations in Figures 3A-I and supplementary figures.

result: Premature eye opening produces modest changes in orientation and direction selectivity. Orientation selectivity was slightly elevated in EO1contra (0.52, p<0.024) and EO2 neurons (0.54, p<0.016) compared to control (0.42), while direction selectivity was slightly reduced in EO1ipsi neurons (0.24, p<0.027) compared to control (0.29). The distributions of preferred orientations and directions did not differ significantly across groups.
evaluation: Claims C4, C23-C31 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical testing (LMEM and chi-square tests). The effects are small but statistically significant for some comparisons, and the authors appropriately characterize these as 'slight' changes. The lack of distributional differences (C30, C31) provides additional context that the changes are quantitative rather than qualitative.

result: Spatial frequency tuning was minimally affected by premature eye opening. No significant differences were observed in peak spatial frequency preferences across groups (control: 0.031 cpd; EO1ipsi: 0.045 cpd, p<0.19; EO1contra: 0.031 cpd, p<0.949; EO2: 0.042 cpd, p<0.362). Low-pass and high-pass indices showed only modest changes, and bandwidth measurements revealed no significant effects.
evaluation: Claims C7, C47-C57 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological measurements with appropriate statistical analyses. The lack of significant differences is well-documented across multiple spatial frequency parameters (peak preferences, low-pass/high-pass indices, bandwidths), providing strong evidence that spatial frequency tuning is relatively preserved despite premature visual experience.

result: Premature eye opening causes long-lasting bilateral increases in spontaneous firing rates. Spontaneous firing rates were markedly elevated in both EO1ipsi (11.1 Hz, p<1.09e-4), EO1contra (6.6 Hz, p<0.0132), and EO2 (6.6 Hz, p<0.0248) hemispheres compared to control (2.6 Hz). This bilateral effect suggests a global change in circuit excitability not restricted to cells viewing through the prematurely opened eye.
evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C68-C73 are strongly supported by electrophysiological data showing significant increases in spontaneous activity across all experimental conditions, including the ipsilateral hemisphere. The bilateral nature of the effect (C5, C6) is particularly compelling evidence for a global circuit change. Statistical significance is robust (p<0.0248 or better), and the interpretation (C73) is reasonable given the persistence of effects measured at P55-68.

result: Peak visual responses were unchanged by premature eye opening (control: 7.0 Hz; EO1ipsi: 6.4 Hz, p<0.600; EO1contra: 10.1 Hz, p<0.518; EO2: 10.5 Hz, p<0.295), but response suppression below baseline was significantly elevated, particularly in EO1ipsi cells (7.0 Hz, p<1.59e-9) compared to control (2.1 Hz).
evaluation: Claims C58-C67 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical analyses. The dissociation between unchanged peak responses and increased suppression is well-documented. The particularly strong effect in EO1ipsi cells (p<1.59e-9) is notable and statistically robust. Figure 5A-B provides visual confirmation of these findings.

result: The authors interpret the temporal frequency tuning deficits as suggestive of motion processing impairments and propose that premature visual experience in ferrets may model aspects of visual deficits observed in very premature human infants. They suggest that broadened temporal frequency tuning could impair discrimination of temporal frequency and speed of moving stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C74, C75, C8, and C103 represent interpretations and extrapolations from the experimental data. While the temporal frequency deficits are well-documented (Result 1), the connection to motion processing (C74, C75) is inferential and would require behavioral testing to confirm. The link to human prematurity (C103) is speculative, though the authors appropriately cite relevant literature (C100-C102). These interpretations are reasonable but not directly tested.

result: The authors speculate that closed eyelids in altricial mammals may serve to protect the developing visual system from high luminance, high contrast, and high spatial frequency stimulation until circuits are ready for visual experience refinement.
evaluation: Claims C9 and C105 are explicitly speculative (C9 states 'we speculate'). While the experimental data showing lasting deficits from premature vision are consistent with this hypothesis, the evolutionary interpretation is not directly tested. The speculation is reasonable given the findings but represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result.

result: The experimental design involved opening ferret eyes at P25 (during retinal wave period), providing 8 hours of visual experience over 4 days, and recording from monocular V1 at P55-68. The study used 27 female ferrets: 17 with one eye opened early, 4 with both eyes opened early, and 11 controls.
evaluation: Claims C16-C20 and C106-C110 describe the experimental methodology and are well-documented in the Materials and Methods section. The timing is appropriately chosen based on cited developmental milestones (C16, C17 supported by citations). The sample sizes and recording locations are clearly stated. The methodology is sound for addressing the research questions.

result: The manuscript establishes the developmental context by citing prior work showing that mammalian visual system development proceeds in two stages: an early experience-independent stage guided by molecular cues and spontaneous activity, followed by an experience-dependent refinement stage. By P42 in ferrets, most visual response properties have reached adult-like levels.
evaluation: Claims C1, C10, C11, C21, C22 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Katz and Shatz 1996; Wong 1999; Li et al. 2006; Chapman and Stryker 1993; Issa et al. 1999). These provide the necessary developmental framework for interpreting the experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work is accurate.

result: The authors contextualize their findings by comparing to prior altered-rearing studies, noting that dark-reared ferrets show poor direction selectivity but not strong temporal frequency deficits, strobe-reared cats show direction and motion sensitivity changes, and temporal frequency tuning is not rapidly modified by brief exposure after natural eye opening.
evaluation: Claims C76-C83 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Imbert and Buisseret 1975; Li et al. 2006; Kennedy and Orban 1983; Ritter et al. 2017; Bissen et al. 2025). The comparisons help establish the novelty of the temporal frequency deficits observed in this study. The characterization of prior work appears accurate based on the citations provided.

result: The authors establish clinical relevance by noting the rising population of very premature human infants who receive visual stimulation during the presensory period, and that such infants exhibit visual deficits including motion perception impairments and sometimes lowered visual acuity, even when brain damage and retinal problems are excluded.
evaluation: Claims C12, C13, C100-C102 are supported by appropriate citations to clinical literature (Crump et al. 2019; Colonnese et al. 2010; Ortibus et al. 2009; Atkinson and Braddick 2007; Jain et al. 2022). The characterization of the clinical population and their visual deficits provides important motivation for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the clinical context is accurately represented.

result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms by noting that visual input can drive activity through closed lids, GABAergic signaling switches occur by P21-23, inhibitory cells show activity patterns associated with orientation columns before eye opening but lack orientation selectivity, homeostatic mechanisms operate during critical periods, and retinal waves show interhemispheric coordination.
evaluation: Claims C85-C96 are mechanistic background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Krug et al. 2001; Akerman et al. 2002; Mulholland et al. 2021; Chang and Fitzpatrick 2022; Desai et al. 1999; Hengen et al. 2013; Bock et al. 2012; Weliky and Katz 1999; Murcia-Belmonte et al. 2019). These provide context for interpreting the bilateral effects and potential circuit-level changes. The citations appear appropriate.

result: EO1ipsi cells exhibited slightly higher temporal frequency preferences (p<0.021) compared to other cell types.
evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by statistical analysis (LMEM, p<0.021) and shown in Figure 3E. This finding is somewhat unexpected given that EO1ipsi cells viewed through the naturally-opened eye, but the statistical support is clear. This may relate to the bilateral effects discussed in Result 4.

result: Prior studies in other species (bobwhite quail and rats) have shown that premature sensory experience causes behavioral and perceptual deficits, including loss of species-specific visual selectivity, altered auditory processing, and asymmetric locomotor reactions.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Lickliter 2018; Sleigh and Lickliter 1995; Foreman and Altaha 1991). These comparisons across species strengthen the generalizability of the finding that premature sensory experience has lasting consequences. The characterization of prior work appears accurate.

result: Ferrets are an appropriate model for studying premature visual experience because they undergo long postnatal development, are born with eyes closed for 30-35 days, and in the wild raise young in relatively dark nests.
evaluation: Claims C14, C15, C84 establish the rationale for using ferrets as a model system. C15 is supported by citation to Issa et al. 1999, and C84 by Ruggiero et al. 1994. The characterization of ferret development and natural history is accurate and provides important context for the experimental manipulation.

result: The authors conclude that premature patterned vision has a long-lasting impact on the development of receptive fields in visual cortex, regardless of clinical relevance to human vision.
evaluation: Claim C104 is a summary statement supported by the collective experimental findings (Results 1-5). The lasting nature of the effects is demonstrated by measurements at P55-68, well after the critical period closure. This is a well-supported conclusion from the experimental data.
